It seems common knowledge that when it comes to vehicles, it's great to know a mechanic and someone who knows what they are doing, else you're liable to be easily fleeced. For some reason, the same has not been held true for PC hardware/software troubleshooting. I think people have a vague idea that they want to have a "techie" type person around. But when it comes to bringing computers in to places, when that nephew or random friend doesn't know how to fix something, they still trust random shops or big box stores. Even still, some people know better on both these fronts, they know to bring their system to someone they trust and they know that big box stores don't always have their best interest at heart. What a lot of people don't know, is that they should now be suspicious of a lot of the big companies behind the products and software they use. For example, Microsoft has gone so incredibly aggressive in their strategy to push Windows 10 on people, that they are now willingly pushing updates to break people's clients, in what I expect is the hope that clueless/helpless PC owners would then give up on their "broken" computers and pay some hack to install the newest "free" copy of Windows 10, to replace their previously perfectly working OS. Alternatively, if you leave your Windows Updates on (as has so often been considered best practice and likely told to you by your resident tech expert), Microsoft has now taken the stance to use THAT system to force Windows 10 to download to your computer. Regardless if you want that update or not, or if you want to install it or not, Microsoft wants you to have it so it's "convenient" when you DO decide to do that upgrade. "But Windows 10 upgrade is free, why wouldn't I want it?" Sure, it's free, have you ever wondered why? Because Microsoft has numerous systems, ingrained on the kernel level, that are almost impossible to remove that use all kinds of subterfuge and shady tactics to gather information about the user, including usage habits etc. That data is valuable, FAR more valuable than the $500 or whatever amount you'd have paid for previous iterations of the OS. Corporations are beginning to go too far, instead of looking out for the customer, they are trying to find ways to dupe them into getting software they don't need, in the name of money. And it's not just Microsoft. How about everyone else's favorite AAA brand, Apple. Recently a guy who uses their Apple Music service found out that through various means of subterfuge in the EULA of the service, Apple was essentially given cart blanche to replace existing mp3 copies of songs he had ripped from his personal library (or in this case created himself) and taken it upon themselves to sync that data with their cloud and remove/delete the tracks from his drive. (see here: https://blog.vellumatlanta.com/…/apple-stole-my-music-no-s…/). Apple, and some media shills are of course blaming the user, for not reading the fine print as well as not understanding how ITunes (or whatever other apple related music app)'s service actually works, that there is ways to prevent this issue etc. The thing is, there ARE solutions to both of these issues, the Windows 7 update that Microsoft is pushing out, that they *know* screws up systems with ASUS motherboards, can be fixed with some settings in the bio, a guide for which has actually been provided by ASUS themselves. The same with Apple's music service, if you can navigate ITunes asinine internals, there is a means to prevent it from removing tracks and/or scanning for existing tracks on your drive to keep your system secure. My qualm is, in both of these cases, the company should be protecting the consumer, at the lowest common denominator. They should not be relying on people to have a high level understanding of the internal workings of drivers or permissions based issues. Because that's not most people. This kind of thing doesn't affect me, because I've had Windows automatic updates disable on my system forever, and taken measures to block all of the known heinous updates on a kernel level so even if somehow the setting returned, the updates could never effectively be installed on my system. But I'm not like most people and even among those technically savvy, the only reason I've taken the time to do this kind of thing is because I have a very strong stance, on principle, against Microsoft and Windows 10's new initiative to gobble up as much personal data as they can. I don't think any of that makes me special, if anything, it's being an exception to a general rule that is why I find it so offensive. Because people shouldn't have to be weird security techno nerds like I am in order to have an expectation that their existing, perfectly working software would not otherwise be tampered with or knowingly broken (which is especially heinous) by the companies which provide it to them, all to make a quick buck. This practice, of trying to screw the vast majority of users, hidden under only the thinnest veneer of "read the EULA" or "You should have known better" is repugnant. In a perfect world, given the ubiquitous nature of tech in our day-to-day lives, everyone would have a stronger fundamental understanding of how it works. I would absolutely love that, but it's not reality and it won't be for another generation or two, until the kids growing up on IPads, Instagram and Twitch start having kids of their own. It is my honest belief, not to sound conspiratorial, that until that day comes, these companies are relying on the general lack of knowledge and know-how to essentially rob and fleece people of their hard earned money. Worse still, is companies like Microsoft, Facebook etc. who are going even BEYOND those measures and trying to dupe people into giving up every last minute detail about their lives so they can be sorted and filed algorithmically in a way that allows these companies to "best" sell them things they don't need, often at exorbitant prices. I guess in the end, this is more of a rant than anything against the prevalence of corporate greed in the tech world. These companies and the people working for them know better. The people in IT helping "fix" issues and charging hundreds of dollars to some poor sap for something they could resolve in 30 minutes know better. The developers working for bleeding edge media and social tech startups farming all your data so they can sell it to the highest bidder know better. I know better and my conscience will no longer allow me to say nothing about it. If something goes wrong with your computer, it may be your fault, especially if you're not "savvy", but don't be too quick to assume it's all on you, because a lot of the companies we once trusted no longer have our collective back. In fact, they are relying on that exactly misplaced trust and lack of savvy to turn a profit. That's fact, not conspiracy, and anyone who tells you otherwise is probably looking to make a buck. Food for thought.
